newsitem.title: RUSSIA: AvtoVAZ plans seen encouraging for foreign buyers.
newsitem.headline: AvtoVAZ plans seen encouraging for foreign buyers.

text.p: Russia's plan to sell half of indebted car giant AvtoVAZ, possibly to a strategic foreign investor, could open talks with a series of foreign carmakers -- provided Russia is ready to let an outsider take control.
Analysts said on Wednesday that the plan, announced by First Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin on Tuesday, was likely to improve investment conditions at AvtoVAZ.

"You are getting closer to the right conditions for a strategic investor. Both the Russian government and AvtoVAZ management have stronger incentives now," said Per Maelstrom, head of research at the Moscow-based Brunswick Group.

But the company was still saddled with huge debts and social responsibilities for its 114,000 workers. It has a poor history of management and marketing and its Lada cars are the subject of a series of dubious jokes.

Potanin, announcing a deal aimed at preventing the start of bankruptcy proceedings at AvtoVAZ, said the auto firm planned a new share issue worth billions of dollars to help pay off its 2.8 trillion rouble ($500 million) tax debt.
The issue could be sold to a single strategic investor or to portfolio investors, he added.
Auto analysts in Moscow said the move showed Russia and VAZ were increasingly willing to talk with strategic investors but stressed that a controlling stake had to be offered.

"If the stake does not have control, it is worth one cent. But if it is a controlling stake, then for a strategic investor to win that market share is potentially worth hundreds of millions of dollars," said MC Securities' Patricia Isayeva.
VAZ, Russia's largest auto maker, is producing about 670,000 cars this year, up almost 10 percent on a year ago.
It has Russia's largest dealer and service networks.

Foreign auto investors General Motors, Ford Motor Co, and Korea's Daewoo and Kia have already announced or begun auto ventures in the former Soviet Union with controlling stakes rather than enter the Russian market as a junior partner.
Potanin, who named Germany's General Motors unit Opel AG, BMW AG and Ford as companies which could be approached as possible investors, did not mention the issue of control.

Interfax news agency quoted the governor of the Samara region, where VAZ is located, as saying VAZ, the region and the federal government had agreed not to sell a controlling stake, but this could not be confirmed.

Maelstrom said VAZ could have a limited value to portfolio investors, one answer to a non-controlling stake, but Isayeva said smaller stakes would increase problems for investors, who would be unable to ensure modernisation.
Analysts said the process would not be solved in two months, when Potanin said VAZ shareholders would discuss the move.
VAZ has already looked for partners on its own. "All the major volume car companies in the world have been to see them," Maelstrom said.
"This will not happen over the next two or three months."
Isayeva said the new search could be easier for VAZ management, forcing the Russian government to use its influence -- and ability to give investment privileges.
"Now VAZ management can say, "we can't find a strategic investor, let the government do it.' Then it is no longer their fault and the government will have the headache."
